prohibited_recommendations: Do not escalate AED dose or add a second AED for events without electrographic correlate.
Do not start a benzodiazepine drip during a PNES event.
Do not intubate prophylactically for events meeting PNES semiology criteria.
Do not dismiss the patient — PNES is a treatable disorder requiring multidisciplinary care.
required_recommendations: Admit for prolonged video-EEG monitoring to capture habitual events — gold-standard diagnostic test.
Identify the precipitating psychosocial trigger (daughter's recent epilepsy diagnosis, maternal guilt) and arrange psychiatric/CBT referral.
Maintain stable lamotrigine for the underlying confirmed epilepsy; do not escalate AED therapy for the PNES events.
Safely taper escalating alprazolam use with addiction-medicine input.
Counsel on driving restrictions given any breakthrough epileptic activity.

accepted: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) coexisting with previously controlled right mesial temporal lobe epilepsy

differential.key_features: Possible but the new semiology is markedly different from prior documented events; video-EEG without electrographic correlate excludes this.
Would require new ictal pattern from a different region; video-EEG and stable MRI rule this in or out.
Lamotrigine level would document subtherapeutic adherence; the contradictory semiology argues against pure breakthrough seizures.
Escalating alprazolam use can produce paroxysmal events on withdrawal; less stereotyped than seizures.
No postural or exertional trigger; preserved awareness during the events excludes loss-of-consciousness-driven syncope.

key_clinical_evidence: PNES and epilepsy coexist in 10–30% of patients followed in chronic epilepsy clinics; both must be addressed.
Marked semiology change from prior stereotyped epileptic events is a high-yield clue (longer duration, closed eyes, side-to-side movement, preserved awareness, no post-ictal confusion).
Video-EEG capturing the event without ictal correlate is the definitive diagnostic gold standard.
A psychosocial precipitant frequently precedes PNES onset; identifying it is therapeutic.
AED escalation in PNES adds toxicity without benefit and may obscure the true diagnosis.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.

July 2026 review applied end to end: routine EEG first when appropriate, staged sleep-deprived/ambulatory escalation, video only for event capture or tertiary evaluation, and continuous ICU EEG only for NCSE.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Dual pathology: PNES coexisting with controlled temporal lobe epilepsy. The known epilepsy creates a strong cognitive anchor that all events are epileptic. Requires video-EEG to distinguish PNES from epileptic seizures, careful semiology comparison, and recognition that AED escalation is harmful for PNES.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Coexistence of two disorders (PNES + controlled epilepsy) requires careful semiology contrasting, video-EEG capture, and avoidance of AED escalation. High risk of anchoring to known epilepsy diagnosis.

patient.history_present_illness: 38-year-old right-handed Hispanic female with a 10-year history of well-controlled right temporal lobe epilepsy (hippocampal sclerosis, on lamotrigine 200 mg BID, seizure-free for 3 years) presenting with a 2-month history of increasing 'seizure' frequency, now 2-3 events per week. She has been to the emergency department 4 times in the past 2 months for these events. However, the semiology of the new events differs significantly from her prior documented epileptic seizures: (1) longer duration — the new events last 5-20 minutes (prior seizures lasted 1-2 minutes), (2) eyes closed during events (prior seizures had eyes open with staring), (3) wild bilateral thrashing with side-to-side head movement (prior seizures had behavioral arrest with oral automatisms — lip smacking and chewing), (4) preserved awareness during some events — she reports remembering everything during the episode, (5) no post-ictal confusion (prior seizures always had 20-30 minutes of post-ictal confusion and word-finding difficulty). The precipitant: 3 months ago, her 16-year-old daughter was diagnosed with epilepsy, causing severe maternal guilt and anxiety. She has been taking increasing amounts of alprazolam.
